extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated general public and scientists seeking popular summaries of research and biography
extracted.subtask_description: A Popular Science Monthly magazine piece summarizing Heidenhain's experimental observations on hypnotism and a biographical sketch of Lewis H. Morgan emphasizing his methods and contributions to anthropology. The text highlights experimental details and standards of careful scientific and inductive research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strictly scientific experimental practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments 'undertaken and prosecuted in a manner strictly scientific' (referring to Braid's investigations and Heidenhain's methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out experiments with scientific care and candor; record methods and observations systematically so results are credible and reproducible. The text praises work 'undertaken and prosecuted in a manner strictly scientific.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication / independent confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings should be confirmed by independent investigators (noted: 'every one of his results confirmed by Heidenhain' regarding Braid's observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek and report independent confirmation of results; replication by other researchers strengthens credibility and supports surprising or incredible findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care and candor in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should be pursued with 'care and candor' even amid opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about methods, limitations, and negative or controversial results; the page emphasizes the moral/scientific value of careful and candid reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic collection and systematization of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather wide-ranging empirical material and organize it systematically (Morgan 'gradually by years of labor thoroughly systematized' materials; kinship systems recorded and tabulated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent data collection, compile and systematize raw materials (tables, schedules) before drawing broad conclusions; present organized evidence to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standardized inquiry instruments (schedules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare and circulate schedules of inquiry to gather comparative data (Morgan prepared schedules circulated among missionaries, teachers, traders, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and distribute standardized forms or questionnaires to ensure comparable data across informants and regions; document distribution and response processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive, fact-based research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research presented as a 'model of inductive research'—building theory from assembled facts rather than speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize empirical accumulation and let generalizations emerge from abundant, organized facts; avoid premature theorizing before data are in hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient, persistent, well-directed labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuing 'many years of patient and well-directed labor' in assembling and analyzing large bodies of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that substantial, reliable contributions often require long-term, consistent effort; plan for extended data-gathering and synthesis phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative breadth and abundant examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims with 'abundant examples throughout the globe' (e.g., kinship systems of eighty tribes and many Old World societies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wide comparative evidence to justify general claims; ensure examples span relevant geographic/cultural variation before asserting universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical inference from wide evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw reasoned conclusions from broad empirical foundations (Morgan 'logically inferred that gentile society... are the universal characteristic of man in his passage through the period of barbarism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base theoretical inferences on systematic, comparative patterns in the data and make the logical steps explicit; avoid leaps unsupported by the assembled evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of sensational or inappropriate terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruct histories 'from existing materials' and avoid being misled by the 'glitter of inappropriate terms' or exaggerated accounts (paragraph on Montezuma and Aztecs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, appropriate terms; resist romanticized or inflated vocabulary that can produce deceptive conclusions; revise terminology to fit evidence rather than force evidence to fit terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful experimental observation and physiological measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypnotism experiments document detailed observable phenomena and physiological correlates: reflex excitability changes, tonic muscle contraction, breathing and pulse rate increases, progressive spread of stimulation following Pfluger's law, mapping sensitive areas (e.g., eyelids, pit of stomach), and use of tuning-fork and unilateral stroking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record detailed behavioral and physiological measures, map stimulus–response relationships, compare responses across stimulus strengths and locations, and note temporal persistence (e.g., reflex excitability persisting days after). Include concrete measurement where possible (breathing rate, pulse, blood volume changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report equivocal results and anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge equivocal or inconsistent findings (e.g., unilateral hypnotism sometimes produced catalepsy on the same side as stroking, sometimes on the opposite; some results were equivocal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit or gloss over inconsistent data; report exceptions, variability, and cases that do not fit the main pattern, and discuss possible reasons or limits to interpretation.
